title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
description: Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or
body:
Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

title: Do the Apple Watch Series 12's New Health Features Live Up to the Hype?
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I now have the Apple Watch Series 12 in my hands—or, rather, on my wrist—and have spent the past 24 hours putting it through as many tests as I can manage. I'm pleased with the step counting and the availability of "recovery HRV" (as opposed to the cardiac-health-focused HRV that the Apple Watch previously used) but I'm not sure if the heart rate accuracy is living up to the hype. I'll be putting this device to more rigorous tests, but here are my first thoughts. 

    
            
            Apple redesigned the heart rate sensor on the back of the watch. Left: Apple Watch Series 11. Right: Apple Watch Series 12
                                        Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                    
    
Step counting is everything I hoped it would beApple waited forever to add step counting as an easily viewable metric on the watch, but it’s finally here. I can open my smart stack (with a double pinch of my fingers, not even touching the watch screen) and see my steps right on top. I’ve also added a step count complication to my watch face. You can find this complication under Activity. The option to see your rings as a complication is still there, but you can now also add steps or wheelchair pushes.Step counts work well. They update quickly, and seem to be accurate in my casual counting—nine steps from my desk to the door registers as nine steps. I’ll do more in-depth testing soon, to properly evaluate Apple’s claim that it now has the most accurate step counting out there. 
What’s disappointing is that it took so long—and that step counting is not coming to the Series 11 or any earlier watch. Apple’s step counting uses a special pedometer model that’s built into its new processor. Older Apple watches don’t have the hardware to calculate your steps as precisely, leading Apple to leave the feature off those watches. That is wild to me, considering that every other wearable has had step counts on the watch ever since the first cave dweller strapped a rock to their wrist. I’m not sure I buy these “most accurate heart rate” claimsApple claims the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate in a wearable, and I’ve already mentioned that that's a bold claim given what I’ve seen in the past from Apple and from other devices. Now that I have a Series 12 in my hands, I was able to do some preliminary testing. To be totally clear, these are not thorough tests, and I’m not making a decisive conclusion based on just a few days’ testing. But I’ll show you what I’ve tried so far. As always, I’m testing the device against my heart rate as read by a chest strap (the gold standard for heart rate comparisons). I did: A treadmill interval run with the Series 11 and a chest strapAn identical treadmill interval run with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the Garmin Forerunner 570 for good measureAn outdoor run that included steady jogging, intervals, and walking, with the Series 12, a chest strap, and the 570. I’m including the 570 in these tests because it has what I would consider the most accurate heart rate sensor in a wearable. In my past testing it’s reported numbers that were identical or nearly identical to the chest strap. That said, there’s always variation from day to day, and it didn’t shine quite as well in these recent tests compared to some I’ve done in the past. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            Apple Watch Series 11, top, and 12, bottom. Red dots are the Apple Watches; gray is the chest strap for reference.
                                        Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                    
    
Here are the indoor runs with the Series 11 on top, and the Series 12 on the bottom, both in red and both compared to a chest strap. The Series 11 was already doing a pretty good job, and to be honest I’m not sure if the Series 12 is any better. I’m disappointed that the Series 12 is still only sampling heart rate every five seconds during workouts. Other devices, like the chest strap and the Garmin, sample every second. That means Apple is taking 12 data points every minute while these other devices are taking 60. 
    
            
            Apple Watch Series 12 in red, Garmin Forerunner 570 in blue, chest strap for reference in gray
                                        Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                    
    
Here’s the outdoor run. The chest strap is in gray, Garmin in blue, and Apple in red. Again, the sparse data points of the Apple watch aren’t impressive. I see a few places where Apple missed the peak of a small spike, but then again the Garmin struggled in a few spots as well. I’ll do further testing and report back when I’ve been able to try out the watch in a greater variety of activities and conditions.What I can’t test yetLive Rewind and Siri Recaps aren’t available yet. Live Rewind is the feature where you can ask for a text transcription of whatever was said around you in the last 15 seconds. Recaps handle a longer timeframe—for example, to summarize a meeting. These features are coming later this year, and aren’t in the version of watchOS 27 that came with the watch. (I have not installed any beta software on the watch.) Readiness is another big feature coming soon, but I haven’t logged enough nights of sleep to get my scores yet—it needs about a week of data. As a preview, I am seeing my “recovery HRV” listed with my sleep data. Last night my HRV was 45 according to Apple, and 50 according to my Oura ring. HRV readings from different devices may vary, depending on exactly when they take their measurements, so I’ll be looking for trends rather than specific data points. If both devices agree on what is a high or a low reading for me, given my baseline, I’ll call that a success for Apple.

title: I Tried 'Tailscale,' the Self-Hosted VPN Service That Makes It Look Like You're Always Home
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Tailscale has apps for all the major device platforms.
                                                    Credit: Tailscale
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Tailscale wasn't on my radar until a friend recently raved about its capabilities to me. Looking around the web, it seems the software has attracted a loyal following; perhaps part of the reason I hadn't come across it before is that it's not all that easy to understand what it does. Tailscale is technically a VPN (Virtual Private Network), but not in the way the term is typically used. Whereas something like NordVPN or ExpressVPN connects you to someone else's network to access the wider web, Tailscale does the opposite, and connects you to your own network from outside.
    
            
            Start your tailnet with one of the apps.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
"Remote access technology" has been around for years, of course, but it often involves a lot of detailed and technical setup steps—you want to be able to access your home network remotely without letting anyone else in, and that usually means some complicated configuration involving router settings and several third-party apps.There's none of that with Tailscale, and when you actually install the software, you quickly start to see what all the fuss is about. You can be sitting in a coffee shop or hotel room and have virtually the same access to your home network as you would if you were actually in your living room, which has all kinds of benefits, from file sharing to managing your smart home devices.
The obvious use case is remote access to a computer you have at home, without the layers of complexity or using another company's servers. Tailscale also makes it easier to access media servers you've set up with apps like Plex or Jellyfin, and smart home setups running through Home Assistant or another dashboard.
    
            
            You can be set up in minutes.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Everything is built on the open-source WireGuard VPN protocol, which creates private and encrypted links to all of the devices you want to connect to your network—your "tailnet." To add a new device, just install Tailscale on it, whether it's your phone on a 5G connection or a desktop computer set up at the office. Tailscale is free for personal use, which covers up to six individual users and an unlimited number of personal devices, though there are some limits: 50 tagged resources (always-on devices that need multi-user access, like a NAS box), and three Access Control List or ACL groups (for setting access permissions per user). Paid plans start at $8 per month.Putting Tailscale to the testThe ease of setup is one of the main appeals of Tailscale, and it couldn't be much more straightforward. Download the relevant app on whatever device you want to start with, create an account (you can sign in using a Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or Apple account), and you're up and running. I had a Windows PC, a MacBook, an Android phone, and an iPhone connected to my tailnet in a matter of minutes, with just a few taps and clicks required. There's also a web portal you can access to see all of the devices you've connected and what they're up to.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            The macOS app offers easy drag-and-drop file sharing.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One improvement I noticed right away was the addition of Tailscale to the share sheet on Android and iOS, which meant I could quickly share photos and other files between all my devices in seconds (no AirDrop or Android Quick Share required). I could also instantly access the shared folders on my desktop and laptop computers from my phone.Something else you can do very easily is set up a remote access app on a phone and use it to connect directly to one of your computers in a different physical location, with no exposure to the wider internet and no advanced configuration required—Tailscale provides you with an IP address that looks like a local network. Any of your home computers can be configured as an exit node as well, which means internet traffic can be rerouted through it. If you're in a hotel, for example, you can use Tailscale as a secure tunnel back home, which means websites see you as visiting from home rather than an unrecognized hotel IP address.
    
            
            Taildrop lets you quickly share files between connected devices.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
There are some areas where Tailscale can improve (the Windows client isn't quite as straightforward to use as the macOS one), and it's fair to say at least some basic networking knowledge is required to get to grips with Tailscale, but in terms of software that's free and useful, it's hard to beat. I didn't dive into more advanced use cases involving NAS drives or home servers, as they're not something that I'm working with at the moment, but that's the next level of Tailscale capability

title: This New iOS 27 Feature May Save You From Getting Scammed
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: LuckyDuck via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Starting with iOS 27, your iPhone now has a built-in scam prevention feature, designed to protect you from social engineering scams. These scams rely on pressure tactics to trick you into bypassing security features for your phone, laptop, or online accounts. Here's how iOS 27's "Impersonation Risk Detection" works, what it can do, and its current limitations.How Impersonation Risk Detection works to protect you from scamsIn a social engineering scam, a bad actor impersonates an official rep of a bank, government agency, or a tech company such as Apple, Google, or Microsoft. The scammer may even impersonate your friends, family members, or colleagues you trust. They'll try to force you to disable account security measures such as two-factor authentication, or talk you into sharing your financial information. They'll create a fake problem, establish trust, and then pressure you into making large payments. Apple says Impersonation Risk Detection can analyze information about your iPhone or iPad, your Apple Account, and check for signs of an active scam. Once it completes the analysis, iOS 27 will share a risk level with the app that's being targeted by scammers. Apple emphasizes that the app doesn't receive any data associated with your device or Apple Account that was used to assess the risk level.
From there, it's up to the app to decide how to proceed. If an app supports Impersonation Risk Detection, it may add a delay to each step you're trying to execute, show warnings, or even ask you to verify your identity. Apps can use various factors to decide if they need a risk assessment from iOS 27, which include big changes to your account, resetting its password, disabling two-factor authentication, making large payments, etc.What are the various risk levels in Impersonation Risk Detection?Once an app requests iOS 27 for a risk assessment, the operating system can conduct an analysis and place the action into one of three risk level markers (again, Apple doesn't control what apps do with the risk level information):Unknown: This means that iOS 27 couldn't detect any suspicious activity. Apple says that doesn't mean the action was confirmed as safe.Medium: This risk level is assigned when iOS 27 detects some signs of suspicious activity.High: This risk level is associated with significant signs of suspicious activity.How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Pranay Parab
                    
    
Once you've updated your iPhone to iOS 27 (or your iPad to iPadOS 27), go to Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and tap Impersonation Risk Detection. Enable the toggle next to "Share with App Developers." Now, tap Share with App Developers in the pop-up. Once Impersonation Risk Detection is enabled, you don't need to take further action. Note that when you try to disable this feature, it may take up to 24 hours to take effect. This is to protect you from scammers, who may pressure you into disabling the feature.In the same settings page, you'll be able to see which app requested access to your risk levels, and why. This will show up under the "Recent Activity" section. You'll also be able to turn off this feature for individual apps that appear in this section, but, again, it may take up to 24 hours to disable the setting.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The limitations of Impersonation Risk DetectionSecurity features are only as strong as their weakest links. In the case of iOS 27's Impersonation Risk Detection, there are two main weak links. First, this feature is disabled by default. Most people aren't going to dig deep enough into settings to discover it accidentally, and the feature isn't going to be used widely unless people know about it. Second, this feature also depends on app developers adding support for it. Big tech companies and indie developers may adopt it reasonably quickly, but other developers may not rush to implement this feature.There's also the fact that plenty of apps have already spent a lot of resources building up their own security infrastructure, and they may not necessarily see value in adding support for this feature. Here in India, all banking and payment apps show multiple full-screen warnings when you try to make a payment while on a phone call. Some apps may even disable payment features if they detect that a screen-sharing app is installed on your device. So, really, it will come down to how app developers respond to this feature.Does Impersonation Risk Detection keep my data private?Apple says that Impersonation Risk Detection performs its analysis on-device, and that the data used to generate the risk level doesn't leave your device. The company also highlights that the contents of your email, photos, or messages are not analyzed for the risk assessment. When an app requests a risk assessment, Apple claims it only receives information about the type of action you performed in that specific app. Once the risk level is generated, apps don't receive any additional data about you.

title: How to Tell If an October Prime Day Deal Is Just Hype
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: zhu difeng/Shutterstock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        October Prime Day is nearly here. For those two days, you’ll find promotions on products from companies both big and small, all vying for your clicks and the contents of your bank account. Many of these offers will claim to be great deals, implying that not buying the item during October Prime Day will mean missing out on massive savings. But not all October Prime Day deals are really all that great—just because a product is discounted on October Prime Day doesn't mean it hasn't been cheaper before, nor that it won't be cheaper later. Fortunately, there are a few strategies you can use to quickly figure out whether that “amazing deal” really is all that.How to tell a good October Prime Day price from a bad oneOne of the best things you can do to tell if an October Prime Day deal is legit is to use a price tracker. These sites and tools keep tabs on the prices for any given product across the many different stores and vendors where it is sold, in order to give you the best possible price, as well as show you whether that current “deal” really is that much lower than the original price or other deals that are out there.A common technique to make deals look good is to pump up the price of the product: That way, when the company slashes the price for something like October Prime Day, it can claim a large discount, even if the overall price tag isn’t much lower than the original price (if it's lower at all). If something originally costs $60, a company can raise the price to $75, then cut it back down to $60, claiming it took 20% off. It’s accurate, but scummy, so watch out for it.You can use a browser extension like CamelCamelCamel to watch a product's price history on Amazon. But other trackers, like Capital One Shopping, can help you find prices and price histories for items across multiple stores. Their browser extensions are especially useful: If there’s another store selling the same product you’re looking at on Amazon for less, you’ll get a pop-up letting you know, with a direct link to that store’s product page.Knowing whether something is a good deal isn’t all about getting the best price, though. You might see that an item isn’t any cheaper elsewhere on the web, but there’s more than just the general price tag to consider.Make sure you’re not unknowingly buying an outdated piece of techI’m a big believer in old tech: I think we should all hold onto our devices for longer. However, I don’t think companies should sell you old tech as if it were new, especially when new tech is right around the corner. Amazon in particular is often helpful here: If you’re looking at an outdated version of a product, Amazon lets you know, and gives you a link to the current version of that device. However, that’s only true if Amazon carries that new version, or if there’s a direct successor to that product. Lines are blurred these days: Last year’s device isn’t necessarily obsolete just because there’s a new version out, so Amazon doesn’t always try to sell you on the newer product.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And that can be fine! Last-generation laptops, tablets, smartwatches, and phones are often great choices. Tech is advancing so rapidly that it can be frugal and practical to buy older tech that still works well. That said, a store telling you to buy something that won’t be able to update to the latest software later this year isn’t right. If you see a deal on the first-gen Apple Watch Ultra, for example, know that you can't update it to watchOS 27—even though the device itself is perfectly usable. If you’re looking to buy a piece of tech on October Prime Day, research is your friend. It’s more than okay to buy something that came out last year or the year before; what matters more is making sure the product will still work as it should in 2026, and if it’ll last as long as you’d reasonably expect it to. If the reason a device is at such a good price is that it’s obsolete, that’s not a good deal. Not everything “cheap” is good On a similar note, be wary of cheap tech that simply isn’t very good. It might be affordable, but if it doesn’t work well, it’s not worth the cost. Often, this issue arises with the many brands you’ve never heard of selling items for pennies compared to other companies. Sure, you could save some money and go with these brands, but what about the long-term investment? If the return policy is up, you’re sunk without a customer support channel, something many of these tiny companies lack themselves. On the other hand, you might have heard of the brand, but the product itself just isn’t very good. It might seem like a steal to get a giant 65-inch 4K TV for less than $300, but if the picture quality is really poor, was that really worth it? (No.)Read the reviewsOne way to make sure that TV is worth its steep price cut, or whether those cheap headphones are going to pass the listen test, is to read reviews for the products you’re considering buying. I’m not talking about Amazon reviews, either: Amazon’s ratings can be helpful, but they can also be compromised. Sometimes the reviews don’t even match the product they’re supposed to be talking about, which doesn’t bode well for the integrity of the review. And in the age of AI, you can never be too sure who's writing that customer review in the first place.When it comes to tech, the best approach is to listen to the reviewers with technical experience, who put these products through their paces before issuing an opinion. Outlets like our sister sites PCMag or CNET will help you figure out pretty quickly whether that TV is really worth the hype, and they show their work so you can understand how they came to their conclusions. At the end of the day, it’s all about taking your time and doing your research—the opposite of the October Prime Day “BUY IT NOW” strategy. Fight the urge to buy something on impulse, and make sure your money is going toward the best possible product for your needs.
